# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Partner]
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Praitir Baking Holdings, LLC / Glailirt Artisan Breads, Inc.: Exposure Review of Transaction Documents
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Scope and Key Dates

I reviewed all six documents in the folder:

- **D1:** Asset Purchase Agreement dated February 9, 2026 (the "APA").
- **D2:** Transition Services Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (the "TSA").
- **D3:** Praitir Board of Managers Unanimous Written Consent dated May 12, 2026 (the "Board Consent").
- **D4:** Bill of Sale dated March 2, 2026.
- **D5:** Closing logistics email thread, February 23 to March 3, 2026.
- **D6:** Kestrel Point payoff and lien release letter dated February 26, 2026.

The most serious problems only appear when two documents are read together.

The dates below drive the analysis:

| Item | Date / Term | Source |
|---|---|---|
| APA signing | February 9, 2026 | APA Preamble |
| **Closing Date** | **March 2, 2026** | Bill of Sale Recital B; Board Consent Recital A; email thread Msg. 19 |
| **TSA Transition Period** | **180 days beginning on the Closing Date** | TSA §1.1 |
| End of Transition Period | About August 29, 2026 | Computed |
| **Rep and warranty survival cut-off** | **About October 28, 2026** (60 days after the Transition Period ends) | APA §9.1, computed |
| Closing Statement delivered | March 30, 2026 | Board Consent Recital C, Res. 2.1 |
| **Notice of Disagreement deadline** | **April 29, 2026** | APA §2.6(b), computed |
| Board Consent authorizing the dispute | May 12, 2026 | Board Consent |
| Expected Copperline Sale closing | On or about July 15, 2026 (inside the Transition Period) | Board Consent Recital E |
| Monthly Service Fee | $142,000 per month | TSA §4.1 |
| Base Purchase Price / Cap | $18,400,000 / $1,840,000 | APA §§2.5, 9.5(b) |
| Governing law | New York | APA §11.6; TSA §12.9 |

**Counting note:** if March 2 is counted as day 1 of the 180, the Transition Period ends August 28 and the survival date falls one day earlier, on October 27. We should treat the earlier date as the operative deadline.

**Status check needed:** the folder runs only through the May 12, 2026 Board Consent. Several deadlines below (July 15 and October 28) may now have passed. Before we contact Glailirt's counsel (Ridgeway Haskell), we should confirm with the client:

- whether the Notice of Disagreement was sent;
- whether the Copperline Sale has closed; and
- whether any Section 9.4 claim notices were served before October 28.

The recommendations below are written for the posture shown in the documents. Where a date has already passed, the remedy shifts from preventing the problem to mitigating it.

---

## 2. Priority Ranking: What Needs Your Attention First

| Priority | Issue | Why it is urgent |
|---|---|---|
| **1: Immediate** | **Issue A:** Closing Statement objection window expired April 29, 2026 (APA §2.6(b)–(c); Board Consent) | The deadline has already passed. About $277,550 of inventory value is in dispute. The board has directed management not to pay, which creates a breach risk. |
| **2: Urgent** | **Issue B:** Copperline Sale is a change of control that gives Glailirt a TSA termination right (TSA §12.2) | Glailirt's consent is not on the Required Consents list. If the sale closes without it, Glailirt can cut off production, QA, logistics and IT services on 10 days' notice. |
| **3: Urgent** | **Issue C:** All Seller reps expire about October 28, 2026 (APA §9.1 + TSA §1.1) | Protective claim notices must go out before the cut-off. The board's May 2026 capex already points to possible environmental rep breaches. |
| 4: High | **Issue D:** Buyer pays occupancy costs of the excluded Secaucus Depot (TSA §4.3 + APA §1.1) | This is a recurring monthly overpayment. We need to dispute each invoice before its due date. |
| 5: High | **Issue E:** Uncapped Buyer indemnity for Seller's pre-closing employee liabilities (APA §§6.8(b), 9.3(c), 9.5(b)) | The exposure is unlimited, but it is contingent. It is a priority item for the amendment package with Glailirt. |

---

## 3. Issues

### Issue A: Notice of Disagreement Window Expired Before the Board Acted

**Where:**
- APA §2.6(b) (30-day Review Period) and §2.6(c) (final and binding effect).
- Board Consent Recital C and Resolution 2 (§§2.1–2.5).

**What the documents say:**
- Under APA §2.6(b), Buyer may deliver a Notice of Disagreement "within thirty (30) days after delivery of the Closing Statement."
- Under §2.6(c), if Buyer does not do so, "the Closing Statement and the Closing Inventory Value set forth in it shall be final and binding on the Parties."
- The Board Consent states that Glailirt "delivered the Closing Statement on March 30, 2026," by email to Praitir's CFO with a courier hard copy.
- The 30-day Review Period therefore ran to **April 29, 2026**.
- The Board Consent authorizing a Notice of Disagreement is dated **May 12, 2026**, 13 days after the window closed.
- Nothing in the folder shows that a notice, extension or waiver was delivered before April 29.

**Why it matters for Praitir:**
- **Size of the dispute.** Glailirt's Closing Statement shows a Closing Inventory Value of $1,326,450 and asserts that Praitir owes **$111,650**. Praitir's own figure is $1,048,900, under which Glailirt would owe Praitir about **$165,900**. The total swing is **$277,550** (Board Consent Exh. B).
- **Finality.** If §2.6(c) applies, Glailirt's figure binds Praitir, and Praitir loses the Independent Accountant process under §2.6(d).
- **Breach risk from non-payment.** Resolution 2.4 directs officers not to pay under §2.6(e). If the Closing Statement is final, the payment was due within 5 Business Days after finality. Withholding it exposes Praitir to a breach claim and to fee-shifting under the "Losses" definition.
- **Waiver formalities.** APA §11.10 requires any waiver to be in writing and signed. Silence or a course of dealing by Glailirt will not rescue the claim.
- **The point is still live.** The board has expressly refused to accept the figure, so this is an active dispute and not a closed issue.

**Recommended fix:**
1. **Today:** confirm whether anything went to Glailirt before April 29. A CFO email disputing the figures, or a request for working papers, might qualify as a Notice of Disagreement or support a waiver argument.
2. **Seek a written extension or waiver.** Ask Glailirt for a signed agreement under §11.10 extending the Review Period, or accepting the Notice of Disagreement as timely. One option is to pair it with a mutual extension of the survival period in Issue C, which Glailirt may want for its own claims.
3. **Argue the Review Period never started.** APA §11.2 governs "all notices... and other communications." It requires delivery to Buyer "Attention: Chief Executive Officer," with a copy to Buyer's counsel. The Closing Statement went by email to the CFO, and the record does not show a copy to Bellmont Arcaro. If delivery did not comply with §11.2, the 30 days arguably never began to run.
4. **Argue Glailirt's access failure.** Under §2.6(b), Glailirt must give access to its working papers during the Review Period. The board only now directs management to request them (Res. 2.4). If Glailirt did not provide them, we can argue the Review Period was tolled or that Glailirt is estopped.
5. **Preserve a fallback indemnity claim.** Several disputed items are expired or near-expiry finished goods and improperly valued butter. These may also breach the Inventory rep in APA §4.10 (shelf life, storage, write-downs). We could pursue them under §9.2(a), but:
   - recovery is subject to the $184,000 Deductible; and
   - §9.8 makes §2.6 the governing mechanism, so Glailirt will argue the indemnity route is barred.
   The claim notice must also go out before the survival cut-off in Issue C.
6. **Hold the non-payment position carefully.** Advise the client that withholding the $111,650 is a litigation position. If Glailirt will not extend, the client should decide deliberately whether to pay under protest.

---

### Issue B: Copperline Sale Triggers TSA Change-of-Control Termination Right

**Where:**
- TSA §12.2 (and §5.1).
- Board Consent Recital E, Resolution 4 and Exhibit A.

**What the documents say:**
- TSA §12.2 provides that "any change of control of Buyer shall be deemed an assignment." This expressly includes "any transfer of a majority of the equity interests." Seller's prior written consent is required.
- If a deemed assignment occurs without consent, "Seller may terminate this Agreement upon ten (10) days' notice to Buyer."
- The Board Consent approves the sale of **100% of Praitir's membership interests to Copperline Fund IV, L.P.**, expected to close on or about **July 15, 2026**. That date falls well inside the Transition Period, which runs to about August 29.
- The Required Consents list (Res. 4.1 and Exhibit A) covers only Hudson Commerce Bank (Credit Agreement §7.11) and Tidewater (Equipment Lease §18.3). **Glailirt's TSA consent is not on it.**

**Why it matters for Praitir:**
- **Operational exposure.** On 10 days' notice, Glailirt could stop all Schedule A services mid-transition, including:
  - production planning (A-1);
  - QA and food safety support (A-2);
  - procurement under non-assigned supply arrangements (A-3);
  - logistics and dispatch (A-4);
  - ERP, order management and route accounting (A-5); and
  - finance support (A-7).
- **Replacement systems may not be ready.** The board only authorized replacement providers in May (Res. 5.3).
- **Food safety and regulatory risk.** Abrupt loss of QA support and the environmental monitoring program would create food-safety and FDA/Ag & Markets risk at the Bronx Plant.
- **Leverage for Glailirt.** Glailirt can use the consent requirement to extract concessions. This is especially likely while the inventory dispute in Issue A is open.
- **No APA exception.** APA §11.4 lets Buyer assign the APA to a purchaser of the Business without consent. The TSA has no matching carve-out, and APA §11.9 makes the TSA control as to the Services.
- **Possible effect on survival.** Glailirt may argue that early termination ends the "Transition Period" early, which would shorten survival under APA §9.1 even further. The better reading is that the Transition Period is a fixed 180-day term under TSA §1.1, but the argument adds risk.
- **MIPA disclosure risk.** If the MIPA has a contracts or no-conflicts representation, failing to flag the TSA consent could create exposure to Copperline.

**Recommended fix:**
1. **Add Glailirt** (TSA §12.2) to Exhibit A Required Consents. Assign a responsible officer, and request the consent by the May 29 timing in Exhibit A.
2. **Obtain a written consent and waiver from Glailirt** before the Copperline closing. It should confirm that the Copperline Sale is not a deemed assignment and waive the §12.2 termination right for that transaction.
3. **Budget for a consent fee.** Note that the board's $75,000 consent-fee cap (Res. 4.2) does not contemplate this consent.
4. **If consent cannot be obtained:**
   - accelerate migration under TSA §2.5;
   - consider terminating dependent services early under §5.2 on Praitir's own timetable; or
   - negotiate with Copperline to make Glailirt's consent a closing condition, or to move the sale closing past about August 29.
5. **In any TSA amendment,** add a carve-out from §12.2 for a sale of Buyer or the Business, mirroring APA §11.4.
6. **Status:** if the Copperline Sale has already closed, confirm whether Glailirt has noticed termination. If not, seek a ratifying waiver now.

---

### Issue C: Seller's Representations Expire About October 28, 2026 (Indemnity Survival Gap)

**Where:**
- APA §9.1 (survival) and §9.4(a) (claim notices).
- TSA §1.1 (definition of "Transition Period").

**What the documents say:**
- APA §9.1 provides that all representations and warranties survive "until the date that is sixty (60) days after the expiration of the Transition Period."
- The APA does not state the length of the Transition Period. APA §1.1 imports the definition from the TSA.
- TSA §1.1 defines the Transition Period as "the period of 180 days beginning on the Closing Date." The Bill of Sale confirms the Closing Date as **March 2, 2026**.
- Read together, the Transition Period ends about **August 29, 2026**, and **every Seller representation expires about October 28, 2026**. That is roughly eight months after Closing.
- Under APA §9.4(a), §9.2(a) claims must be noticed before that date. Neither document shows the problem on its own.

**Why it matters for Praitir:**
- **The affected reps carry latent risk.** The cut-off applies to the reps that matter most for a commercial bakery:
  - environmental compliance and releases, including FOG/high-strength wastewater discharges and grease interceptors (§4.16(a)–(c));
  - the combustible flour dust hazard analysis under NFPA 652/61 (§4.16(d));
  - food safety, FDA and pathogen history, and recall history (§4.19);
  - condition of assets (§4.8), inventory (§4.10), tax (§4.21) and employment/WARN (§4.17).
  These are latent risks that typically surface after inspections, testing or a recall, often years after closing.
- **Fundamental reps are caught too.** The Fundamental Representations (title, authority, organization, brokers) are subject to the same cut-off. Section 9.5(c) removes the Cap and Deductible for them but does not extend their survival.
- **Far shorter than the statutory period.** New York's six-year limitations period for contract claims (CPLR 213) would otherwise apply. New York courts generally enforce contractual survival limits, so the shortened period should be treated as binding.
- **Possible breaches are already visible.** In May 2026, the board approved capex to upgrade the flour-silo dust collection system "in accordance with the recommendations of the Company's combustible dust consultant," and to replace the grease interceptor (Res. 6.1). This sits uneasily with:
  - §4.16(c), which represents that there are no grease interceptors in disrepair; and
  - §4.16(d), which represents that the dust hazard analysis recommendations were implemented.
  These are potential claims that will be lost if not noticed in time.
- **Partial mitigation.** Pre-Closing environmental liabilities (§2.4(f)) and pre-Closing product and recall liabilities (§2.4(e), §10.2) are Excluded Liabilities. They are indemnified under §9.2(c), which §9.4(a) does not tie to the survival date, and covenants survive indefinitely under §9.1. Glailirt will still contest that route, and pure rep breaches have no fallback. Examples include compliance failures without a third-party liability, asset condition, inventory and permits.

**Recommended fix:**
1. **Send protective notices now.** Serve written claim notices under §9.4(a) and §11.2 before the survival date, and ideally well before October 27. They should cover every known or suspected rep breach, including:
   - dust collection and the dust hazard analysis (§4.16(d));
   - the grease interceptor (§4.16(c));
   - the inventory items in Issue A (§4.10); and
   - any Form 483, environmental monitoring or wastewater sampling findings since Closing.
   Each notice must have "reasonable specificity" so the claim survives under the last sentence of §9.1.
2. **Amend APA §9.1** to decouple survival from the TSA:
   - general reps: at least 18–24 months after the Closing Date;
   - environmental (§4.16), food safety/regulatory (§4.19), tax (§4.21) and employment/benefits (§§4.17–4.18) reps: at least 5–6 years, or the applicable statute of limitations plus 60 days;
   - Fundamental Representations: the full statute of limitations (six years) or longer.
3. **Fallback if the amendment is not agreed.** Obtain a tolling and standstill agreement. Also amend §9.1 to state that early termination of the TSA under §12.2 or §5.3 does not shorten the Transition Period for survival purposes.
4. **If the date has passed** with no notices served, assess:
   - claims under §9.2(c) (Excluded Liabilities);
   - claims under §10.2 (recalls); and
   - fraud and willful misconduct claims, which are carved out of §9.8 and the Cap.

---

### Issue D: Buyer Reimburses Occupancy Costs of the Excluded Secaucus Depot

**Where:**
- TSA §4.3 (occupancy costs) and §1.2 (imports APA definitions).
- APA §1.1 (definition of "Facilities"), §2.2(d) (Excluded Assets) and §11.9 (order of precedence).

**What the documents say:**
- APA §1.1 defines "Facilities" as "the Bronx Plant and the Secaucus Depot." This works for Seller's property and environmental reps (§§4.9, 4.16).
- APA §2.2(d) makes the Secaucus Depot Lease, and Seller's leasehold and personal property at the depot, **Excluded Assets** that Seller keeps.
- APA §2.4(b) makes liabilities relating to the depot lease Excluded Liabilities.
- TSA §1.2 imports APA definitions. TSA §4.3 then requires Buyer to reimburse "all rent, utilities..., real estate taxes, insurance premiums allocable to the premises, and repair and maintenance costs of the Facilities" during the Transition Period. These amounts "shall form part of the Service Fees."
- APA §11.9 provides that the APA controls over Ancillary Agreements "except that the Transition Services Agreement shall control as to the Services and the Service Fees." The Excluded Asset treatment in the APA therefore does not override TSA §4.3.

**Why it matters for Praitir:**
- **Praitir is paying for a depot it did not buy.** It pays the rent, utilities, taxes, insurance and maintenance of the Secaucus Depot. Seller kept the depot and uses it for its own retail bakery-café distribution (APA §6.7(a)).
- **The rent component is almost all Secaucus.** Praitir already owns the Bronx Plant in fee (APA §2.1(a)), so the "rent" Seller is passing through is effectively Secaucus rent alone.
- **The cost is on top of the base fee.** These amounts come on top of the $142,000 Monthly Service Fee for about six months.
- **Praitir cannot simply net the overpayment.** TSA §4.7 bars set-off except for invoice amounts disputed under §4.5. Amounts paid without a timely dispute (before the payment due date) are harder to recover.

**Recommended fix:**
1. **Dispute invoices immediately.** Instruct the COO (the Service Coordinator, Res. 5.2) to dispute all Secaucus amounts in each TSA invoice in writing before the due date under TSA §4.5. TSA §4.5 bars Seller from suspending services over a good-faith dispute.
2. **Amend TSA §4.3** so that "Facilities," for TSA purposes, means the Bronx Plant only. Limit reimbursement to the Bronx Plant utilities and charges that remain in Seller's name during the transition. Also correct the APA §1.1 cross-reference.
3. **Recover past payments.** Demand a refund of all Secaucus amounts already paid. Grounds include APA §10.3 (wrong pockets), the Excluded Liability allocation in §2.4(b), and Seller's indemnity in §9.2(c).
4. **Audit the invoices.** Use the TSA §3.3 records right to quantify depot charges for the full Transition Period.

---

### Issue E: Uncapped Buyer Indemnity for Seller's Pre-Closing Employee Liabilities

**Where:** APA §6.8(b), §9.3(c), §9.5(b) (see also §2.3(c) and §9.3(d)).

**What the documents say:**
- **What Buyer takes on.** Section 6.8(b) makes Buyer responsible for "all Liabilities with respect to accrued but unused vacation, paid time off and sick pay, all severance and separation pay, and all Liabilities under the WARN Act, in each case relating to the Business Employees, **whether arising before, on or after the Closing Date**."
- **Assumed and indemnified.** Section 2.3(c) makes these Assumed Liabilities. Section 9.3(c) requires Buyer to indemnify Seller for "all Losses described in Section 6.8."
- **No cap.** The Cap in §9.5(b) applies only to "Losses... under Section 9.2(a) and Section 9.3(a)." Neither the Cap nor the Deductible reaches §9.3(c) or §9.3(d), so **Buyer's indemnity is uncapped**. No single clause states this result.

**Why it matters for Praitir:**
- **Scope of the obligation.** Praitir is an unlimited indemnitor of Seller's own pre-Closing employee obligations, including:
  - Seller's accrued vacation and PTO balances;
  - severance owed when Seller terminated all Transferred Employees at Closing (§6.8(a));
  - severance for Business Employees who declined offers; and
  - any federal or New York WARN liability arising from Seller's pre-Closing actions or the Closing-day terminations. NY WARN has a 90-day notice requirement and a lower coverage threshold.
- **No price protection.** None of this was priced as a purchase price reduction in the documents. The exposure is unlimited, while Seller's own indemnity for rep breaches is capped at $1,840,000.
- **The obligation overrides Seller's reps.** It undercuts Seller's reps in §4.17(a) (all compensation paid) and §4.17(c) (WARN compliance). Even if Seller breached those reps, the §6.8(b) allocation and §9.3(c) indemnity point the liability back to Praitir.

**Recommended fix:**
1. **Narrow §6.8(b)** to (a) post-Closing liabilities for Transferred Employees and (b) accrued vacation and PTO for Transferred Employees only to the extent reflected on the updated Disclosure Schedule §4.17 and credited dollar-for-dollar against the Purchase Price.
2. **Keep pre-Closing liabilities with Seller.** Expressly make all pre-Closing severance, accrued compensation and WARN liabilities (including Closing-day terminations by Seller) Excluded Liabilities under §2.4. Strike "before, on or" from §6.8(b).
3. **Bring §9.3(c) (and §9.3(d)) under the Cap,** or impose a separate dollar cap, so Buyer's exposure is no broader than Seller's.
4. **Add a Seller indemnity** under §9.2(c) for pre-Closing employee claims, with a carve-out from the Deductible.
5. **Price the remaining exposure.** Ask the client for current accrued PTO balances and any severance or WARN claims raised since Closing.

---

## 4. Documents Reviewed With No Material Issues

- **Bill of Sale (D4).** Consistent with the APA. It confirms the March 2, 2026 Closing Date and the 12:01 a.m. Effective Time, excludes the Excluded Assets (§3.2), and disclaims any assumption of liabilities (§4.1). It is relevant mainly as the source of the Closing Date used in Issue C.
- **Email thread (D5).** Closing logistics only. It confirms the Closing, the funds flow, the wire call-backs, the permit and regulatory handling for the §7.2(g) condition, and post-closing title and UCC delivery. One point for Issue A: Glailirt sent the Estimated Closing Inventory Value to the CFO by email (Msg. 8). That suggests a course of dealing Glailirt will cite against our defective-delivery argument.
- **Kestrel Point payoff letter (D6).** The math reconciles: $2,272,647.19 plus the $46,000 installment equals $2,318,647.19. The releases cover:
  - the New York Department of State UCC-1 and amendments;
  - the Bronx County fixture filing; and
  - the three vehicle titles.
  Per the email thread (Msgs. 20–22), payment was confirmed, the UCC-3s were filed, and the titles were delivered. Sections 5.2–5.4 bar recourse to Praitir. No action needed.

---

## 5. Suggested Next Steps

1. **Today:** confirm the status of the Notice of Disagreement, the Copperline closing and any §9.4 notices. Then prepare a letter to Ridgeway Haskell requesting:
   - an extension or waiver of the §2.6(b) Review Period; and
   - Glailirt's §12.2 consent to the Copperline Sale.
2. **This week:** serve protective §9.4(a) claim notices (dust collection, grease interceptor, inventory). Have the COO begin disputing Secaucus charges under TSA §4.5.
3. **Amendment package to Glailirt,** covering:
   - APA §9.1 survival;
   - APA §§6.8(b) and 9.3(c), and the §9.5 Cap;
   - TSA §4.3 and the "Facilities" definition; and
   - a TSA §12.2 sale-of-Buyer carve-out.
   Glailirt's own interest in a longer survival period for its claims against Praitir may give us a trade.
4. **Board follow-up:** amend Exhibit A Required Consents to add Glailirt, and revisit the $75,000 consent-fee cap.

Please let me know if you would like draft language for the amendment package or the notice letters.

### Issue 2: The Copperline Sale triggers the TSA change-of-control clause (URGENT)

**Where it appears**
- TSA §12.2. Any "change of control of Buyer shall be deemed an assignment," including "any transfer of a majority of the equity interests." If a deemed assignment occurs without Seller's prior written consent, Seller "may terminate this Agreement upon ten (10) days' notice."
- TSA §5.1: the term runs until the end of the Transition Period unless earlier terminated "under this Section 5 or Section 12.2."
- Board Consent Recital E, Resolution 3, Resolution 4 and Exhibit A. These describe the sale of **100% of Praitir's membership interests to Copperline Fund IV, L.P.**, expected to close on or about **July 15, 2026**.

**What the documents show**
- The TSA Transition Period is **180 days beginning on the Closing Date** (TSA §1.1). From March 2, 2026, it runs to about August 29, 2026.
- The Copperline Sale falls squarely inside that period.
- The board's Required Consents list (Resolution 4.1 and Exhibit A) covers only:
  - Hudson Commerce Bank under Credit Agreement §7.11; and
  - Tidewater under Equipment Lease §18.3.
- **Seller's TSA consent is not listed.** Nothing suggests it has been requested.

**Why it matters for Praitir**
- Closing the Copperline Sale without Seller's consent would let Seller end every Service on ten days' notice. That includes:
  - production planning (A-1);
  - QA and food-safety support (A-2);
  - procurement under Seller's unassigned supply arrangements (A-3);
  - logistics and dispatch (A-4);
  - ERP, order and route-accounting systems (A-5); and
  - finance support (A-7).
- For a bakery that ships every day, losing A-5 and A-4 on ten days' notice would interrupt order intake and deliveries.
- Losing A-2 mid-transition creates food-safety and FDA compliance risk.
- Resolution 5.3 authorizes replacement vendors, but those contracts are not yet in place.
- Seller's leverage is high. It could demand fees or concessions for consent, and it could use the same leverage against Praitir on the inventory dispute in Issue 1.
- The risk also flows back into the MIPA. Copperline will likely require Praitir to perform its material contracts and to give interim operating covenants. A TSA termination could breach those covenants or give Copperline a closing-condition or indemnity claim.
- Early termination of the TSA may also shorten the Transition Period. That would pull the APA survival cut-off in Issue 3 even earlier, since it is keyed to the "expiration of the Transition Period."

**Recommended fix**
1. Add Seller's TSA consent as **Required Consent No. 3** on Exhibit A, with the CFO or COO responsible. Use the same request-by and obtain-by deadlines.
2. Obtain a written consent and waiver from Seller under TSA §12.2 before the Copperline Sale closes. The consent should:
   - confirm the Copperline Sale is not a prohibited assignment;
   - waive the §12.2 termination right for this transaction; and
   - confirm the Transition Period and Service Fees are unchanged.
3. As part of the same amendment, seek to narrow §12.2 so that a change of control of Buyer is not a deemed assignment, or at least so that consent "shall not be unreasonably withheld." APA §11.4 already lets Buyer assign to a purchaser of the Business without consent, and the TSA should match.
4. Flag the issue to deal counsel on the MIPA. They should either add Seller consent as a closing deliverable or allocate the risk in the MIPA.
5. Speed up the replacement-vendor contracts under Resolution 5.3 as a contingency.
6. If the sale has already closed without consent, review at once whether Seller has served any notice. Prepare a waiver-by-conduct argument based on continued performance and acceptance of fees, keeping in mind the TSA §12.3 written-waiver clause.

### Issue 3: Representation survival is tied to the TSA and ends around October 28, 2026 (HIGH)

**Where it appears**
- APA §9.1. All of Seller's representations and warranties survive "until the date that is sixty (60) days after the expiration of the Transition Period."
- APA §1.1. "Transition Period" takes its meaning from the TSA. The APA does not state the length anywhere.
- TSA §1.1. The Transition Period "means the period of 180 days beginning on the Closing Date."
- Bill of Sale Recital B. The Closing Date was March 2, 2026.
- APA §9.4(a). Claims under §9.2(a) must be noticed before the §9.1 survival date.

**What the documents show**
- Reading the documents together, the Transition Period ends on or about **August 29, 2026**.
- Survival of every representation therefore ends on or about **October 28, 2026**, roughly eight months after Closing.
- This applies to all representations without exception. It covers:
  - Fundamental Representations, including title (§4.7);
  - environmental representations (§4.16), including wastewater/FOG discharge permits, ammonia refrigeration and combustible flour-dust/NFPA 652 compliance;
  - food-safety and FDA representations (§4.19), including the pathogen, recall and Form 483 history;
  - tax (§4.21) and employment (§4.17) representations.
- Neither document shows the problem alone. The APA never states a duration, and the TSA never mentions survival.

**Why it matters for Praitir**
- Latent environmental contamination (grease interceptor, wastewater, refrigerant releases) and regulatory findings at a commercial bakery often surface well after eight months. Examples include a DEP enforcement action, an OSHA dust citation, or an FDA inspection tied to pre-closing practices.
- A pre-closing product problem can also surface late, such as an allergen-labeling or Listeria issue.
- Praitir's capital plan (Resolution 6.1) already targets the dust collection system and the grease interceptor. These are the same areas covered by §4.16(c)–(d) and may point to pre-closing non-compliance.
- Without this clause, New York's six-year contract limitations period would generally govern. The clause cuts Praitir's protection to a fraction of that.
- The Fundamental Representations and tax representation would normally survive for the full limitations period. Here they do not, even though §9.5(c) exempts them from the Cap.
- Any early termination of the TSA, under §12.2 (Issue 2) or §5.3, could shorten survival further. Under the clause as written, a TSA extension under §5.4 would lengthen it. Neither result has anything to do with the risk being allocated.
- Some protection does not depend on §9.1. The §9.2(c) indemnity for Excluded Liabilities (§2.4(e)–(f), covering pre-closing product and environmental liabilities) and the §10.2 recall reimbursement are covenant-based and should survive under the covenant language in §9.1. Seller can be expected to argue otherwise for claims that overlap with a representation.

**Recommended fix**
1. **Immediately:** assemble any known or suspected representation breaches and serve written claim notices under §9.4(a) before October 28, 2026. Candidates include the dust collection, grease interceptor and inventory shelf-life findings, plus anything from the environmental and QA reviews. A timely notice preserves the claim under §9.1 until it is resolved.
2. Negotiate an APA amendment that removes the link between survival and the TSA and sets fixed periods:
   - general representations: 18–24 months after the Closing Date;
   - environmental (§4.16) and food safety/regulatory (§4.19): at least 36 months, or until 60 days after the statute of limitations;
   - Fundamental Representations and Taxes (§4.21): 60 days after expiry of the applicable statute of limitations.
3. Confirm in the amendment that the §9.2(c) indemnity for Excluded Liabilities and the §10.2 recall obligations survive indefinitely and are not limited by §9.1.
4. If Seller refuses, consider R&W or environmental insurance, or a holdback against any amounts Praitir owes Seller.

### Issue 4: Buyer's employee-matters indemnity is uncapped and reaches Seller's pre-closing liabilities (HIGH)

**Where it appears**
- APA §6.8(b). Buyer is responsible for all accrued vacation, PTO, sick pay, severance and separation pay, and WARN Act liabilities for Business Employees, "whether arising before, on or after the Closing Date."
- APA §2.3(c). Section 6.8 liabilities are Assumed Liabilities.
- APA §9.3(c). Buyer indemnifies Seller for "all Losses described in Section 6.8, including all Liabilities for which Buyer is responsible under Section 6.8(b)."
- APA §9.5(b). The **$1,840,000** Cap (10% of the $18,400,000 Base Purchase Price) applies only to "Section 9.2(a) and Section 9.3(a)."

**What the documents show**
- The Cap does not reach §9.3(c), so Buyer's employee indemnity has **no cap**. The Deductible in §9.5(a) applies only to Seller.
- The coverage is not limited to Transferred Employees or to post-closing periods. It reaches all Business Employees and liabilities arising **before** Closing.
- That includes severance owed by Seller to employees who did not transfer, and any WARN liability from Seller's own pre-closing workforce actions.
- No single clause states this result. It appears only when §§6.8(b), 9.3(c) and 9.5(b) are read together.

**Why it matters for Praitir**
- Praitir has become an unlimited indemnitor of Seller's own pre-closing employee liabilities. Examples:
  - accrued compensation built up under Seller's management;
  - severance Seller owes to Business Employees who did not accept offers; and
  - federal and New York WARN exposure. New York WARN applies to smaller employers and requires 90 days' notice, and the liability can be significant.
- §6.8(b) conflicts with the general allocation of pre-closing liabilities to Seller in §2.4(a). Because §2.3(c) expressly makes §6.8 liabilities Assumed Liabilities, the specific provision is likely to control.
- The Copperline diligence team will likely spot this as an uncapped contingent liability, which could affect price or indemnity terms in the MIPA.

**Recommended fix**
1. Amend §6.8(b) so Buyer is responsible only for accrued vacation and PTO of **Transferred Employees** that is honored after Closing, in the amounts shown on Disclosure Schedule §4.17 as updated at Closing.
2. Ideally, credit those amounts against the Purchase Price.
3. Move all severance, separation and WARN liabilities arising from Seller's actions on or before Closing, and all liabilities for employees who did not transfer, into **Excluded Liabilities** under §2.4.
4. Amend §9.5(b) to bring §9.3(c) (and ideally §9.3(d)) under the Cap, or set a separate, lower cap for employee matters.
5. In the meantime, quantify the actual exposure: Seller's severance practices, the headcount of non-transferring Business Employees, and any pre-closing layoffs. Seller represented in §4.17(c) that there were none in the 90 days before signing.
